function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "A comparison table of key cleanliness parameters between sand-cast aluminium and wrought extruded bar, covering: PoDFA inclusion content (mm2/kg), bifilm index (mm), hydrogen content (mL/100g), typical Fe level, oxide skin characteristics, and overall suitability as atomization feedstock. Include columns for: Parameter, Wrought Extruded Bar (6063), Undegassed Sand Casting, Degassed/Filtered Sand Casting, and Notes/Source. Include rows for: PoDFA total inclusions, Bifilm index (RPT), Dissolved hydrogen, Bulk oxygen, Fe content, Surface oxide, and Overall feedstock risk."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Parameter | Wrought Extruded Bar (6063) | Undegassed Sand Casting | Degassed/Filtered Sand Casting | Notes/Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PoDFA total inclusions | About **0.01 mm²/kg** as a general wrought-aluminium benchmark; not a guaranteed value for the specific bar. | **0.34–3.13 mm²/kg** before refining in scrap-containing industrial Al–Mg–Si melts; PoDFA may undercount large bifilms. | **0.05–1.11 mm²/kg** after flux refining; typical reduction about **70%**, but commonly still above the wrought benchmark. | PoDFA is a melt-sample metric, not a direct assay of a finished cup. Typical inclusions include Al₂O₃, MgO, MgAl₂O₄, Al₄C₃, refractory debris and TiB₂ agglomerates. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |
| Bifilm index (RPT) | **No defensible finished-bar value**; wrought processing may close or fragment pores but does not prove the absence of oxide films. | Around **≥100 mm** in one highly contaminated, chip-rich melt; this is a comparative poor-quality condition, not a universal sand-casting value. | About **38–42 mm** after intensive rotary or ultrasonic degassing in the same comparative study. | BI is summed pore length on an RPT section and responds jointly to bifilms and hydrogen. It cannot be converted directly to inclusions/kg, and RPT misses closed, uninflated films. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000034) |
| Dissolved hydrogen | Solid-Al equilibrium solubility near the melting point is approximately **0.036–0.046 mL/100 g**; actual bar requires LECO measurement and may be lower. | Common air- or gas-furnace melt: about **0.30–0.45 mL/100 g**; equilibrium liquid solubility near 660 °C is approximately **0.67–0.69 mL/100 g**. | Approximately **0.10–0.15 mL/100 g** is achievable in reported Ar-purging and degassing trials. | Green-sand moisture, humid combustion products, wet cores, coatings and tools can raise hydrogen. The liquid-to-solid solubility decrease promotes porosity. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000047) |
| Bulk oxygen | **No reliable ppm benchmark found** for commercial 6063 extrusion; low PoDFA does not directly establish low total oxygen. | **No defensible universal ppm value**; expected to be higher and more variable because oxide skins, bifilms, dross, spinel and sand-derived oxides are imperfectly measured. | Inclusion burden is reduced, but **equivalence to wrought-bar bulk oxygen has not been demonstrated**. | Molten aluminium forms amorphous alumina essentially immediately in an oxygen-bearing atmosphere. Bulk oxygen, PoDFA and BI measure different populations and should not be interconverted. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000034) |
| Fe content | AA 6063 chemistry is controlled by the supplier; use the bar certificate and OES/ICP result as the baseline. | Begins with charge chemistry but may rise through mixed scrap and uncoated ferrous tooling; **no defensible universal wt%/h pickup rate was found**. | Degassing and filtration remove gas and inclusions, **not dissolved Fe**; chemistry remains charge- and tooling-dependent. | Repeated recycling tends to accumulate Fe and can generate Fe-rich intermetallics. Measure each foundry batch rather than assuming it remains 6063. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031) |
| Surface oxide | Freshly machined metal carries a thin, rapidly re-formed native oxide; the surface is comparatively smooth and readily solvent-cleaned. | Rough, folded and chemically heterogeneous skin that may contain alumina/spinel, adhered or penetrated sand, burnt binder, dross and oxide laps. | Melt treatment improves internal cleanliness but **does not clean the mould-contact skin**; machining remains necessary. | Exact sand-cast reaction-layer thickness is process-specific and was not established by the retrieved evidence. Sand casting can cause metal penetration, while incompletely dried moulds and coatings generate gas and oxidized bubble trails. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047) |
| Overall feedstock risk | **Low and reproducible** when alloy-certified, freshly machined and cleaned; the preferred baseline for composition-spread experiments and a 0.5–0.7 mm nozzle. | **High and poorly bounded** because of bifilms, hydrogen porosity, sand/binder debris, chemistry drift and nozzle-blockage risk. | **Moderate**; potentially acceptable only with certified charge, dry moulds and cores, quiescent pouring, rotary-Ar degassing, filtration, full machining of mould-contact surfaces and lot testing. | Atomization references report about **50–200 ppm O** for well-controlled VIGA powder and **100–500 ppm O** broadly for inert-gas-atomized powders. EIGA avoids crucible-derived ceramic inclusions; these are powder benchmarks, not cast-cup acceptance limits. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039) |


*Table: Comparison of wrought 6063 bar with untreated and melt-conditioned sand-cast aluminium as remelt feedstock. Values are study-specific benchmarks; unavailable universal quantities are identified explicitly rather than inferred.*

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Practice | Effect on Cleanliness | Quantitative Impact (where available) | Practical Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rotary Ar degassing | Removes dissolved H by bubble flotation and can float agglomerated inclusions; poor rotor practice or a surface vortex can create fresh bifilms. | Melt H can fall from roughly **0.35–0.45 to 0.10–0.15 mL/100 g**. In one high-oxide melt, prolonged rotary treatment reduced RPT bifilm index from about **≥100 to 38 mm**, although BI is not a direct H assay. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000034) | Use the lowest effective rotor speed, keep the rotor submerged, prevent vortexing, use dry high-purity Ar, skim gently, degas before final filtration, and pour promptly. |
| Flux injection (RFI) | Wets and separates oxide agglomerates, assists flotation, and can remove alkali and alkaline-earth impurities; it may introduce Na, K, Ca, Cl, or F residues if poorly selected or overdosed. | Industrial Al–Mg–Si trials reduced total PoDFA inclusions from **0.34–3.13 to 0.05–1.11 mm²/kg**, typically by about **70%** and by as much as **92%**. (pqac-00000012) | Use an Al–Mg–Si-compatible flux, dose by melt mass, allow separation, remove dross without remixing it, and verify residual Na, Ca, and K. Flux-free Ar degassing plus filtration may better protect composition-spread experiments. |
| Ceramic foam filtration | Captures refractory fragments, sand, oxide agglomerates, and other inclusions by depth and cake filtration; it does not remove dissolved H, Fe, Cu, or Zn. | Filtered A356 and A319 melts exhibited less porosity; ceramic filtration has also improved aluminium-alloy fluidity by as much as **25%**. Efficiency depends strongly on pore size, priming, and flow. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000045) | Install downstream of degassing and near the mould, provide adequate head, prevent bypass, and preheat and dry the filter. Damaged, wet, or chemically attacked filters can introduce H or inclusions. |
| Bottom-gated or naturally pressurized gating (Campbell rules) | Keeps the system full and fills upward with less splashing, aspiration, free-surface folding, and bifilm entrainment than uncontrolled top pouring. | Keep ingate or free-surface velocity below approximately **0.3–0.5 m/s**. A spin-trap design at **0.43–0.50 m/s** was subcritical, whereas **0.63–1.0 m/s** caused splashing and reoxidation. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043) | Use a tapered sprue, runner extension or spin trap, generous radii, gates below the cavity, and no waterfalls. Validate velocity by simulation or water modelling; naturally pressurized gating alone does not guarantee quiescent flow. |
| Tilt pouring or low fall height | Maintains a short, attached stream and minimizes jet impact, air entrainment, and repeated rupture of the oxide skin. | One model predicted about **1,021 bifilms/mm³** for a **1.5 m** transfer fall and **464/mm³** for a **1 m** transfer. Even **0.3 m** produced modeled damage comparable to six minutes of rotary degassing at 460 rpm; these are model-dependent estimates. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020) | Bring the ladle lip close to the basin, begin slowly, maintain a continuous stream, and avoid stop–start pouring. Tilt or counter-gravity filling is preferable where available. |
| Sand and core drying | Reduces H pickup and gas defects from mould moisture, solvents, core binders, and mould washes; it also reduces spitting and oxidized bubble trails. | No universal H reduction is available. The proposed green sand contains **3–4% water**, while untreated air- or combustion-furnace melts commonly contain about **0.30–0.45 mL H/100 g**. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000047) | Green sand cannot be fully dried while remaining green sand. Use the lowest controlled moisture, dry washes completely, bake no-bake cores, preheat tools and chills, and verify moisture and loss on ignition. |
| Coated tools and dedicated crucible | Limits Fe pickup from bare steel, cross-alloy Zn and Cu contamination, refractory or carbon transfer, and carryover of old dross. | No defensible universal **wt% Fe/h** or Mg-loss-per-melt value was found; rates depend on temperature, contact area, coating condition, agitation, and hold time. Repeated recycling nevertheless accumulates Fe and other persistent residuals. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) | Use BN- or refractory-coated tools, inspect coatings every heat, minimize immersion time, dedicate crucibles and tools to 6xxx or high-purity Al, and assay every heat. Degassing and filtration cannot remove dissolved Fe, Cu, or Zn. |
| Permanent mould in graphite or steel instead of sand | Eliminates sand grains, clay moisture, and binder pyrolysis while producing a smoother, more reproducible surface with less mould-generated gas and reaction-layer contamination. | No direct universal PoDFA or H comparison was found for an otherwise identical cup. Its principal advantage is eliminating sand and core contamination rather than removing inclusions already present in the melt. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000047) | A coated steel or graphite mould with a removable core is likely cleaner than sand for a cylindrical cup. Preheat and dry it, prevent soldering or carbon pickup with a suitable coating, and retain quiescent bottom or tilt filling. |
| Vacuum or inert-gas melting and casting | Reduces exposure to water vapour, lowers hydrogen partial pressure, limits new oxidation, and facilitates H desorption; it does not reliably remove existing entrained oxide films. | Well-controlled VIGA powder is reported at roughly **50–200 ppm O**, versus about **100–500 ppm O** for inert-gas-atomized powder generally. These are powder outcomes, not cast-cup acceptance limits. (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038) | Use a dry, leak-tight system and **99.999% Ar** where powder oxygen matters. Charge clean dense metal under inert cover, avoid violent pressure reduction, and filter before casting. EIGA avoids crucible contamination but requires pre-alloyed rod. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) |
| Argon-shielded pouring | Suppresses fresh oxidation of the pouring stream and advancing free surface, reducing oxide-film nucleation sites for pores. | In A356 trials, Ar-shielded pouring reduced pore volume fraction, number density, and pore size relative to normal pouring, although PoDFA did not reliably resolve the oxide-film difference. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001) | Shield the melt surface, ladle stream, and mould inlet. Use low-flow dry Ar that displaces air without disturbing the stream, and combine shielding with low fall height because inert gas cannot compensate for turbulent handling. |


*Table: Practical controls for approaching wrought-bar cleanliness when producing aluminium cups by casting. Quantitative effects are included where supported, while process-dependent evidence gaps are stated explicitly.*

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):

List of drug names to generate or filter results.

    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: CONTEXT. We make sealed aluminium "cups" as the charge for a vacuum-induction ultrasonic
atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder: induction melting in a graphite crucible with a boron-nitride
wash, chamber pumped down then backfilled with argon to ~150-200 mbar, melt at ~800-850 C
pushed by ~0.2 bar argon overpressure through a 0.5-0.7 mm graphite nozzle onto a 40 kHz
sonotrode plate) to make Al-Si powder (target 15-63 um) for laser powder bed fusion and alloy
studies. Today each cup is machined on a lathe from extruded 3/4 in (19 mm) AA 6063-T52 bar:
70 mm long with a 12.7 mm blind bore 57 mm deep (or a 15.9 mm bore and 1.5 mm wall for a
thin-wall version), filled with 6-16 g of gas-atomized AA 4047 (Al-12Si) powder, and closed
by a press-fit 6063 plug with a ~1 mm vent hole (0.013-0.020 mm interference). Three to five
cups (~150-250 g in total) are melted per run. The runs are a Si composition spread (0-30 wt%
4047 powder in 6063) whose composition is computed from the weighed masses, so the cup metal's
own composition and cleanliness matter. The cups exist to put the powder inside bulk metal so
that it melts in contact with liquid, without loose-powder losses and with little oxide
pickup. Current practice: dry or light-oil machining, a 99% IPA flush, and an 80 C dry.

PROPOSAL. To make larger cups (more powder per cup), students are considering sand casting
them instead of machining: melting aluminium (most likely re-melted 6063 offcuts and scrap,
or commercially pure aluminium, or a casting alloy such as A356) in a clay-graphite or SiC
crucible in a university foundry (gas or electric furnace, melting in air, possibly with no
rotary degassing or flux), and hand-pouring into green sand (clay-bonded, ~3-4% moisture) or
chemically bonded no-bake sand moulds with a sand core forming the cavity. The cast cup might
be used as cast, or with only the bore and the plug seat machined.

QUESTION 1 (oxygen, hydrogen and purity). Quantitatively, how does a sand-cast aluminium part
compare with extruded wrought bar of the same alloy as a remelt feedstock, in terms of:
(a) entrained oxide films (bifilms), dross and spinel (MgAl2O4 in Mg-bearing alloys such as
6063): oxide inclusion content by PoDFA, LAIS, LiMCA, K-mold or reduced-pressure test
(mm2/kg, inclusions per kg, bifilm index) and bulk oxygen in ppm; how it depends on pouring
practice (turbulence, gate velocity above ~0.5 m/s, fall height), on the number of remelts,
and on melting in air versus under inert gas;
(b) hydrogen: pickup from mould moisture, humid air, and crucible or tool dressings; typical
hydrogen (mL/100 g) in undegassed versus rotary-degassed melts and in extruded bar; the
resulting gas porosity; and what happens to that hydrogen and porosity when the part is
re-melted under vacuum and then argon (outgassing during pump-down, melt spitting or
bubbling, hydrogen and internal porosity in the atomized powder);
(c) process contamination: Fe pickup from uncoated steel ladles, skimmers and stirring rods
(rates in wt% per hour at 700-750 C); Si or C pickup from crucibles; sand grains and binder
residues embedded in the surface (burn-on, metal penetration); carbon and nitrogen from
organic binders; Na, Ca, K, Cl and F from fluxes and degassing tablets; Mg loss by oxidation
(wt% per melt); Zn and Cu from mixed scrap;
(d) the as-cast surface: thickness and nature of the oxide skin on sand-cast versus machined
aluminium, and how much of the skin must be machined away to reach clean metal;
(e) the effect of feedstock oxide and hydrogen content on atomization: clogging of sub-mm
nozzles by oxide films and inclusions, powder oxygen content, satellite or irregular
particles, internal powder porosity, and any cleanliness specifications for gas- or
ultrasonic-atomization feedstock (e.g. VIGA or EIGA ingot or rod requirements);
(f) the practices that bring a casting close to wrought-bar cleanliness: drying sand and
cores, rotary argon degassing, fluxing, ceramic foam filters, bottom-gated or tilt pouring
(Campbell's casting rules), coated tools, a dedicated crucible, vacuum or inert-gas casting,
and permanent-mould (graphite or steel) casting instead of sand.
Give numbers with citations, and say plainly where the evidence is thin or only indirect.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Metal foams offer attractive properties for lightweight structures. This study presents the development of a powder metallurgical aluminum alloy intended for foamable wires that can be used in additive manufacturing processes such as wire and arc additive manufacturing (WAAM). Unlike established aluminum wrought alloys, whose melting range is not well suited for foaming, or cast alloys which are not easily extruded into thin wires, the custom AlMg2Si1.2 alloy developed in this study combines a melting interval matched to the decomposition of pre-oxidized blowing agent (TiH
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) with a low alloying content suitable for high extrusion ratios. For this, the alloy composition was determined using thermodynamic calculations. The material was then cast into billets, which were extruded into rod electrodes. Pre-alloyed metal powder was produced from these electrodes using electrode induction melting inert gas atomization (EIGA), and the influence of atomization gas parameters on powder properties was investigated. Increasing the gas pressure from 16.8 bar to 23.0 bar reduced the median particle size from 51 to 40 µm. The best flowability was observed for the fraction 63–90 µm. A solidus temperature of 560 °C and a liquidus of 646 °C were determined by differential scanning calorimetry, aligning with the principal hydrogen-release peak of the blowing agent. Foam samples produced from the powder confirmed the material’s foamability, reaching porosities of 64–68%, as determined by X-ray microscopy. These results indicate that AlMg2Si1.2 processed via EIGA yields reproducible, highly porous foams, and is a suitable basis for foamable wires in WAAM.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Scrap-based melting is essential to the decarbonization of foundry production, but scrap selection is still often treated as a purchasing decision rather than as an integrated metallurgical design problem. This structured critical narrative review evaluated an audited corpus of 105 publications published from 2020 to August 2026. Evidence coding identified 40 aluminum-focused studies, 25 steel-focused studies, 7 cast-iron studies, 7 copper-alloy studies, 1 nickel-base study, and 25 cross-cutting contributions. Only 15 studies were industrial or pilot demonstrations, whereas 55 were laboratory studies and 35 were models, reviews, or contextual analyses. Nominal chemistry alone was consistently insufficient to determine scrap fitness: origin, size distribution, bulk density, coatings, oxide load, entrained contaminants, sampling uncertainty, and furnace-specific response jointly controlled metallic yield, energy demand, melt cleanliness, residual-element accumulation, emissions, and off-specification risk. The review proposes a normalized mass-balance formulation, probabilistic chemistry constraints, a cost-per-tonne-of-conforming-metal objective, and a four-gate scrap-to-alloy framework.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Rotary furnaces remain important in secondary aluminum production because they can process oxidized, coated, low-density, contaminated, and dross-rich feeds that are difficult to recover in conventional bath furnaces. Their flexibility creates a recovery–residue trade-off: heat, rotation, and chloride–fluoride fluxes can liberate and coalesce metal droplets, but may also increase oxidation, emissions, refractory attack, and salt-slag generation. This structured critical narrative review evaluates a coded corpus of 106 publications from 2020 to August 2026. Retrospective A–E classification was performed by one reviewer and represents interpretive judgments of industrial transferability. No level-A repeated industrial campaign with closed aluminum–salt–energy–quality balances was identified. Accordingly, the proposed nine-gate Feedstock–Flux–Furnace–Residue framework is a testable decision architecture rather than a validated control model; low-salt and salt-free strategies remain feed-specific and require prospective industrial validation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In the low-carbon global aluminum cycle actual perspective, the need of remelting aluminum is in constant increase. The objective of this work was to build a portable aluminum foundry based on local materials. This foundry can be used to make small spare parts in complete safety and/or as practical melting equipment. The foundry is made up of a butane combustion Furnace and various tools for handling molten aluminum. The Furnace was manufactured by recycling a defective gas cylinder. After removing the top of the bottle, we lined the inside with a layer of local clay which serves as a 5-centimeter thermal insulator. The crucible was made by recycling a waste hermetic compressor, and the tools by recycling scrap metal. The tests carried out allowed to melt used cans and other parts of motorbikes and cars defective in aluminum. Liquid aluminum was cast to obtain cylindrical and prismatic blanks for machining, as well as other small mechanical parts. The cost of carrying out the project has been estimated at nearly 150,000 XAF.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Increasing the post-consumer recycled content (PCRC) of aluminum automotive body sheet (ABS) is a promising pathway to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from ABS production. However, progress is constrained by the limited end-of-life vehicle (ELV) ABS scrap available and the compositional mismatches between contaminated scrap streams and alloy specifications. This study identifies cross ABS life cycle strategies that sheet mills, automotive OEMs, and recyclers can implement and quantifies their effects using a composition-specific dynamic material flow analysis to model sheet demand and scrap availability coupled with a linear optimization framework that determines annual PCRC potential under product-demand, scrap-supply, and alloy-composition constraints. A supply chain emissions model links PCRC gains to GHG reductions. By 2050, ABS scrap from U.S. ELVs could supply up to 33% of the ABS ingot demand needed to meet U.S. requirements for ABS components, yet PCRC remains negligible under business-as-usual (BAU) strategies due to compositional incompatibilities. Effective strategies to increase the PCRC include: (1) sheet mills developing high-residual-content (HRC) “recycle-friendly” alloys; (2) OEMs shifting 5xxx-series component designs to 6xxx alloys; and (3) recyclers either extracting sheet-rich sub-assemblies before shredding or adopting advanced sorting technologies to separate shredded ELV aluminum scrap by alloy series. Achieving a PCRC that approaches the physical maximum (33%) occurs only when multiple stakeholders act to implement complementary strategies. The combination of ELV scrap sorting by alloy series and deployment of HRC alloys is particularly effective. Together, these measures could raise PCRC to 28% by 2050, increase total scrap content (including production scrap) to 76%, and cut annual ABS component supply chain emissions by up to 42%.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Gas atomization is a key technology for producing high-quality metal powders, widely adopted in additive manufacturing and other powder-based industries due to its versatility and productivity. Its complexity, such as intense gas&ndash;liquid momentum exchange, thermal gradients in solidification, and multiple influencing factors, poses significant challenges for process control. This comprehensive review explores the complexities of gas atomization technology in metal powder production, examining the underlying mechanisms, simulation techniques, flow field dynamics, and key influencing factors. It clarifies that primary atomization is characterized by liquid film atomization, driven by Kelvin&ndash;Helmholtz instabilities, and fountain atomization, triggered by Rayleigh&ndash;Taylor instabilities. Secondary atomization, on the other hand, is predominantly influenced by shear and inertial forces. The review emphasizes the key roles of physical gas and liquid properties, temperature, pressure, nozzle design, and solidification processes in determining the characteristics of the resulting metal powder. It concludes that a thorough understanding of these factors is essential for refining the atomization process and improving the quality of the metal powder produced. The review suggests that future research should focus on resolving discrepancies in atomization mechanisms, enhancing simulation methodologies, and investigating the effects of advanced nozzle designs on the production of metal powder.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>The growing demand for sustainable manufacturing practices has catalysed interest in integrating recycled materials into additive manufacturing (AM) processes. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Superalloys such as Inconel 718 are the preferred materials for highly stressed components in turbine jets as they offer a combination of high strength and excellent resistance to oxidation and corrosion. Despite their exceptional properties, these materials are subject to intense wear, thermal cycling and high-temperature oxidation during operation, which results in high costs and poses risks to safety-critical components. Cold gas spraying presents a promising and very flexible method for coating and repairing such components. However, there are still significant gaps in our understanding of how process guidance influences coating formation and the resulting properties. In this study, the influence of different handling parameters of the robotic motion system (specifically the spray angle, standoff distance, and traverse speed) on the mechanical coating properties (microhardness, porosity, and roughness), the tensile strength, the microstructure formation, and the tribological performance during high-pressure cold gas spraying of Inconel 718, utilizing nitrogen as the process gas, was investigated. It has been found that the spray angle is the most critical factor influencing the deposition rate, the microstructure / porosity, the tensile strength, and the roughness of the coatings, whereas the microhardness remained unaffected. At the lowest spray angle of 90°, significant coating defects and lowest deposition rate were observed. Coatings applied with varying spray angles were also examined for their sliding wear and friction properties. The primary wear mechanism identified was abrasion, characterized by the presence of aluminum oxide debris within the wear track. No significant influence of the spray angle on the wear behavior of the coatings was observed.</jats:p>

W. and Bogdanoff, Toni", title = "Bifilm generation in metal handling and degassing: Total numbers, sizes and damage", year = "2026", journal = "Unknown journal", month = "Sep", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10838912/v1", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10838912/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC" } Abstract: Abstract

Oxide bifilms are increasingly recognised as the dominant defects governing the quality and performance of cast aluminium alloys. However, conventional Reduced Pressure Testing (RPT) only detects bifilms that inflate during solidification, thereby underestimating the true bifilm population. This study develops a theoretical framework to quantify bifilm generation during two critical melt-treatment operations: melt transfer and rotary degassing. Models based on Weber-number-controlled bubble entrainment and breakup were used to estimate bifilm formation rates and characteristic defect sizes. Under typical industrial processing conditions consisting of two melt transfers and rotary degassing, a minimum bifilm concentration of 1,577 mm -3 was predicted, with melt transfer identified as the principal source of defect generation. Experimental assessment of bifilm populations using focused ion beam serial sectioning and three-dimensional reconstruction revealed approximately 187,500 hidden oxide defects mm -3 , exceeding predictions by more than two orders of magnitude. Incorporation of daughter-bubble formation increased the estimated concentration to approximately 6000-8000mm -3 , but a substantial discrepancy remained, indicating that many bifilms likely pre-exist in primary aluminium feedstock. A damage-factor model that combines defect size, numbers, and tensile specimen geometry further demonstrated that melt-transfer operations are considerably more damaging than degassing. Furthermore, degassing becomes more damaging at a certain rotation rate, supporting a change in current rotary degassing practice.

Ultrasonic Acoustic Cavitation Driven Hydrogen Degassing in Molten Aluminium Alloys and Its Effects on Porosity and Mechanical Properties Valid Text Names: 'bhojak¹2026ultrasonicacousticcavitation pages 1-4', 'bhojak¹2026ultrasonicacousticcavitation pages 4-7', 'bhojak¹2026ultrasonicacousticcavitation pages 7-11' BibTex: @article{bhojak¹2026ultrasonicacousticcavitation, author = "Bhojak¹, Kedar N. and Jain¹, Naresh and Nayak², Saroj Kumar and Satpathy², Bijoy Kumar and Bhatt, Nilesh", title = "Ultrasonic Acoustic Cavitation Driven Hydrogen Degassing in Molten Aluminium Alloys and Its Effects on Porosity and Mechanical Properties", url = "https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10859875/v1", doi = "10.21203/rs.3.rs-10859875/v1", publisher = "Springer Science and Business Media LLC", year = "2026", month = "Oct", journal = "Unknown journal" } Abstract: Abstract

High-intensity ultrasonic treatment of molten aluminium alloys generates acoustic cavitation — transient formation and collapse of micro-bubbles in the melt — which provides a powerful physical mechanism for dissolved hydrogen removal without the use of halogen or toxic process gases. This study presents a systematic investigation of the ultrasonic molten metal treatment system applied to AA-series aluminium alloys during continuous strip casting. Experiments were conducted at melt temperatures from 680°C to 760°C with ultrasonic frequencies of 19–21 kHz and varying power densities. The density index (DI) was measured before and after treatment using the reduced pressure test (RPT). Metallographic analysis of transverse cross-sections of cast foil and billet samples was performed to characterise porosity distribution, pore morphology, and grain size. Vickers hardness measurements were taken at multiple positions across the cross-section. Results demonstrate that ultrasonic treatment achieves a density index below 0.08 cc/100g — below the threshold required for defect-free 6-micron aluminium foil production — compared to greater than 0.15 cc/100g observed without treatment. Porosity elimination and grain refinement via the Hall-Petch mechanism are attributed to cavitation-induced degassing and acoustic streaming effects. Hardness uniformity across the cross-section improved by 22% compared to rotary degassing controls. High-intensity ultrasonic treatment of molten aluminium alloys generates acoustic cavitation — transient formation and collapse of micro-bubbles in the melt — which provides a powerful physical mechanism for dissolved hydrogen removal without the use of halogen or toxic process gases. This study presents a systematic investigation of the ultrasonic molten metal treatment system applied to AA-series aluminium alloys during continuous strip casting. Experiments were conducted at melt temperatures from 680°C to 760°C with ultrasonic frequencies of 19–21 kHz and varying power densities. The density index (DI) was measured before and after treatment using the reduced pressure test (RPT). Metallographic analysis of transverse cross-sections of cast foil and billet samples was performed to characterise porosity distribution, pore morphology, and grain size. Vickers hardness measurements were taken at multiple positions across the cross-section. Results demonstrate that ultrasonic treatment achieves a density index below 0.08 cc/100g — below the threshold required for defect-free 6-micron aluminium foil production — compared to greater than 0.15 cc/100g observed without treatment. Porosity elimination and grain refinement via the Hall-Petch mechanism are attributed to cavitation-induced degassing and acoustic streaming effects. Hardness uniformity across the cross-section improved by 22% compared to rotary degassing controls. The system eliminates the use of hex chloride and hexafluoride process gases, which are 24,000 times more damaging than CO₂ as greenhouse agents. Industrial validation was performed with nil pinholes and holes observed in 6-micron foil output and confirmed by two industrial institutions.

The excerpt provides PoDFA and microscopy evidence for oxide-related inclusions in A356 sand-casting experiments, but it does not compare oxide inclusion content with wrought/extruded bar and does not report bifilm index, LiMCA measurements, or bulk oxygen ppm. PoDFA analysis was considered ineffective for reliably quantifying oxide-film content in the base metals or distinguishing oxide levels between pouring methods. Possible reasons were that oxide films were too small for standard inclusion-cake analysis or passed through the PoDFA filter. The reported PoDFA values for UBC normal versus high-surface-area pouring were: Al4C3 (≤3 µm), 0.26 versus 0.03 mm²/kg; MgAl2O4, 0.22 versus trace; (TiV)B2, 0.06 versus trace; and TiB2/TiC, 1.46 versus 0.79 mm²/kg. Micrometer-scale structures believed to be oxide films were observed, with oxygen near the structure approximately twice the matrix level. Oxygen-rich regions were also associated with pores. Argon-shielded pouring reduced pore volume fraction, number density, and size, suggesting reduced oxide-film formation, fewer available nucleation sites, and delayed pore nucleation. The excerpt contains no data on gate velocity, fall height, or number of remelts, so their effects cannot be determined here.

The excerpt describes how oxide-film content was intentionally varied in directionally cast A356 aluminum, but it does not provide numerical oxide-inclusion values or comparisons between sand-cast aluminum and wrought/extruded bar. Three pouring conditions were used: argon-shielded pouring to produce low oxide-film content, normal pouring for a medium or baseline level, and high-surface-area pouring for increased oxide generation. In the latter case, melt passed through a coarse foam filter, which broke the stream into multiple streams and increased the liquid surface exposed to oxidation; the text also notes that reduced stream momentum could affect oxide entrainment. Melt cleanliness was assessed using porous disc filtration analysis (PoDFA), with inclusion content calculated from the inclusion area divided by filtered melt mass and reported in mm²/kg. The supplied excerpt does not report bifilm-index, LiMCA, bulk-oxygen ppm, or PoDFA results, nor does it discuss gate velocity, fall height, or the effect of remelting. Therefore, it supports qualitative conclusions about pouring practice and oxide formation only, not the requested quantitative cross-process comparison.

Abstract:
This literature overview examines the capacity of using aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) rather than conventional grey solid iron in brake rotor packages. Driven by the preference for lighter and more environmentally friendly vehicles, AMCs offer several benefits, including decreased weight, advanced thermal properties, superior put-on resistance, and an optimized breaking system. Studies have concluded that AMCs can gain weight reductions of up to 60% compared to cast iron, resulting in stepped-forward gas performance and automobile management. Besides exhibiting superior thermal conductivity and lower thermal enlargement, it results in better heat dissipation and a reduced danger of warping and cracking. The advantage of using ceramic reinforcements, which include SiC, Al2O3, and B4C, is that they can enhance the damage resistance of AMCs, leading to a longer service life for brake rotors. The review covers various elements of AMC brake rotor development, Starting with manufacturing strategies (stir casting, ultrasonic-assisted stir casting, and squeeze casting), which are powerful techniques for producing extremely good AMC rotors, then the thermal traits, which are so essential due to their thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, and heat dissipation in brake rotor overall performance, Finally, the tribological residences affect load, sliding pace, and floor roughness on the wear and friction of AMC rotors. Brake pad compatibility is so vital in breaking systems, that deciding on suitable brake pad materials, containing non-asbestos organic (NAO) pads, can optimize performance with AMC rotors. These traits can be computationally analysed by using finite element evaluation and different numerical methods to predict the thermal and mechanical behaviour of AMC brake rotors. The review emphasizes that AMCs maintain great promise as next-era manufacturing for brake rotors, offering a balance of weight reduction, stepped-forward thermal control, and more advantageous wear resistance. Further research and improvement are necessary to optimize fabric composition, production strategies, and brake pad compatibility to improve the capacity of AMCs in brake structures.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Abrasive wear remains a critical challenge in tooling and manufacturing processes, as it leads to accelerated material loss, reduced component life, and increased operational costs. This complex phenomenon is governed by dynamic contact conditions, plastic deformation, fracture, and the properties of both the material and interacting abrasive particles. This study uses finite element analysis (FEA) to investigate abrasive wear behavior of JIS SKD11 tool steel coated with Ti- and Cr-based hard coatings, including TiN, TiAlN, CrN, and AlCrN. A single-asperity scratch model was developed to simulate the ploughing wear mechanism, incorporating strain-rate sensitivity via a modified Johnson-Cook model. The simulation results, validated against experimental data, showed good agreement in surface profiles. Wear performance was assessed using degree of wear (ß) and degree of penetration (Dp). TiN exhibited the lowest penetration and highest plastic deformation, indicating strong wear resistance. CrN offered the best substrate protection, while AlCrN showed the highest material loss due to brittle failure. Overall, the findings highlight the critical role of coating selection in improving abrasive durability and demonstrate the potential of advanced FEA-based approaches for optimizing protective coatings in tool steel applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
With the rapid development of the electric vehicle market since 2012, lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries face retirement intensively. Numerous LFP batteries have been generated given their short service life. Thus, recycling spent LFP batteries is crucial. However, published information on the recovery technology of spent LFP batteries is minimal. Traditional separators and separation theories of recovering technologies were unsuitable for guiding the separation process of recovering metals from spent LFP batteries. The separation rate of the current method for recovering spent LFP batteries was rather low. Furthermore, some wastewater was produced. In this study, spent LFP batteries were dismantled into individual parts of aluminium shells, cathode slices, polymer diaphragms and anode slices. The anode pieces were scraped to separate copper foil and anode powder. The cathode pieces were thermally treated to reduce adhesion between the cathode powder and the aluminium foil. The dissociation rate of the cathode slices reached 100% after crushing when the temperature and time reached 300℃ and 120 min, respectively. Eddy current separation was performed to separate nonferrous metals (aluminium) from aluminium and LFP mixture. The optimized operation parameters for the eddy current separation were feeding speed of 1 m/s and magnetic field rotation speed of 4 m/s. The separation rate of the eddy current separation reached 100%. Mass balance of the recovered materials was conducted. Results showed that the recovery rate of spent LFP can reach 92.52%. This study established a green and full material recovery process for spent LFP batteries.

Abstract:
Stainless steel is one of the most commonly used structural materials in industry for the transportation of liquids such as water, acids, and organic compounds. Corrosion is a major concern in industry due to the use of strong mineral acids, feedstock contamination, flow, aqueous environments, and high temperatures. Stainless steel is the most commonly used material in the petrochemical industry because of its characteristics of self-protectiveness, offered by thin passive oxides, and its metallurgical composition. However, chlorides and mineral acids attack the stainless steel continuously, consequently breaking down the passivation film, causing a continuous challenge from corrosion. The corrosion in stainless steel is influenced by many factors including flow rate, temperature, pressure, ethanol concentration, and chloride ion content. This review describes the impact of organic compounds and organic acids on the degradation behavior of stainless steel. The review also summarizes the commonly used organic compounds and their applications. It has been demonstrated that organic acid concentration, temperature, and halide impurities have significant effects on susceptibility to pitting corrosion by damaging the passivation film. The phenomenon of corrosion in stainless steel is quite different in immersion tests and electrochemical potentiodynamic polarization. This review article discusses the importance of organic compounds and their corrosion behavior on steel. The article also puts emphasis on the roles of corrosion inhibitors, monitoring methods, corrosion management, and forms of corrosion.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Recycled metals have become a strategic resource for the casting industry in the transition toward sustainable manufacturing and circular material flows. This review summarizes the present understanding of using 100% recycled alloys in foundry applications, covering microstructural evolution, mechanical properties and energy efficiency. The aim is to make an integrated assessment of the scientific findings and industrial practices that underpin the wider adoption of recycled feedstock in metal casting. This review summarizes what is known about the influence of impurities, oxide formation and melt treatment on the resultant microstructure. Various observations are reported that trace impurities of alloying elements may modify the dendritic morphology, eutectic phases, and porosity of recycled metals; often these can be minimized by proper refining and filtration. The mechanical performance results vary depending on the alloy type, recycling route and melting practices; nevertheless, a considerable number of research findings prove that tensile strength, hardness and fatigue resistance of castings manufactured from 100% recycled feedstock remain comparable to those produced from primary metals when proper process control is applied. This review also points out the importance of melt cleanliness, degassing procedures and alloy chemistry stabilization in achieving consistent quality. Overall, the collected research indicates that 100% recycled metals can be effectively integrated into the casting processes and are an essential part of sustainable foundry operations. In this context, the utilization of recycled metals brings considerable benefits in terms of energy consumption reduction, minimizing carbon emissions, and supporting circular economy principles. This review is expected to help future studies and industrial practices by summarizing challenges, key technological developments, and opportunities for full-scale implementation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The cleanliness of aluminium alloys has a decisive effect on their properties and performance. In this work, the melts of several Al-Mg-Si alloys (6xxx series) were refined using rotary flux injection (RFI) of the salt fluxes in the industrial environment. A typical charge consisted of 25 % to 30 % external scrap, 45 % to 50 % internal scrap, and 20 % to 30 % primary aluminium. During injection, the entire melt volume was mixed uniformly. The melt was filtered using a porous ring filtration apparatus. The fraction and type of non-metallic inclusions were determined using light and scanning electron microscopy. The contents of alkali and alkaline-earth metals were determined using optical emission spectroscopy. The reduction of alkali and alkaline earth metals and the fraction of non-metallic inclusions were used to evaluate the process efficiency and the flux selection for the regular production. An analysis of more than 100 industry charges confirmed that the flux selected after the experimental trials, consisting of a mixture of MgCl2, KCl, NaCl and CaF2, was effective in regular production.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000012

From text 'kovacec2025removalofinclusions pages 3-4'.

Uroš Kovačec and Franc Zupanič. Removal of inclusions and trace elements from al-mg-si alloys using refining fluxes. Strojniški vestnik - Journal of Mechanical Engineering, 71:294-300, Oct 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.5545/sv-jme.2025.1371, doi:10.5545/sv-jme.2025.1371. This article has 3 citations.

The excerpt provides PoDFA inclusion measurements before and after flux treatment, rather than a separate, standardized dataset specifically for filtration and degassing. Reported total inclusion levels before treatment range from 0.34 to 3.13 mm2/kg, and after treatment from 0.05 to 1.11 mm2/kg. The corresponding reductions range from approximately 50% to 92%, with the text stating that the typical reduction was about 70%. For inclusions excluding grain-refiner debris, values range from 0.26 to 2.18 mm2/kg before treatment and 0.01 to 0.62 mm2/kg afterward. The article notes that industrial filtration is normally performed immediately before casting, but that reducing inclusions before filtration is desirable because inclusions can block the filter. Identified inclusion types include Al2O3 oxide inclusions, furnace-lining MgAl2O4 spinel, TiB2 particles or agglomerates from Al-Ti-B grain-refiner debris, Al4C3 formed through reaction with organic substances, and MgO associated with magnesium and atmospheric oxygen. Regarding material origin, the excerpt specifically links recycled/remelted scrap with grain-refiner debris and TiB2 inclusions; it does not provide a direct quantitative comparison with primary wrought ingot aluminium. Thus, the data support a qualitative distinction, not definitive primary-versus-recycled benchmark levels.

## pqac-00000013

From text 'gerrard2014inclusionsandhydrogen pages 62-68'.

AJ Gerrard. Inclusions and hydrogen and their effects on the quality of direct chill cast and flat rolled aluminium alloys for aerospace applications. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt provides general PoDFA inclusion-level benchmarks rather than a complete before-and-after filtration/degassing comparison. ## pqac-00000017

The excerpt models bifilm generation during aluminium melt transfer as gas entrainment caused by a falling, pouring jet impacting the receiving melt surface. The entrained gas-to-melt volume ratio is correlated with the Laplace number and Weber number, approximately as QAir/QMelt = 7.00 × 10^-4 La^0.273 We^0.901 (the equation formatting is partly corrupted in the excerpt). The Weber number depends on jet diameter and impact velocity, We = ρDJv/σ. Impact velocity is related to fall height through Torricelli’s law, v = √(2gh), so increasing fall height raises gate/jet velocity and Weber number, thereby increasing oxide-film entrainment. The model then uses a critical Weber number of approximately 1.2 to estimate the maximum bubble—or bifilm—diameter: DT = 1.2σ/(ρ√(2gh)). The number of bifilms per unit melt volume is obtained by dividing the entrained air volume fraction by the volume of an individual bubble, represented by N = (QAir/QMelt)/[(4π/3)(DT/2)^3]. Thus, turbulent pouring can create a large population of small bifilms, with the predicted number governed by entrainment, melt properties, jet dimensions, and impact velocity. The excerpt does not state or derive a specific critical gate velocity of 0.5 m/s; that value would require information from another section or source.

The excerpt describes recycling and remelting in aluminum alloys primarily as an alloy-specific impurity-control problem. Iron is identified as a central constraint in Al–Si foundry alloys because it accumulates during recycling and promotes Fe-rich intermetallic phases; these can impair ductility, feeding, and machinability. The severity of Fe pickup depends on silicon and manganese levels, cooling rate, modification practice, and the required property envelope. Recycling can also introduce copper, zinc, magnesium, nickel, oxides, coatings, moisture, inclusions, dross, and contamination from machining chips or thin scrap. The text emphasizes that oxidation and contamination may dominate recovery even when incoming scrap chemistry appears compatible, so preparation, compaction, process route, and segregation are important. It does not provide numerical values for Fe pickup from steel tools, Mg loss per remelt, or impurity accumulation rates. It also does not quantify magnesium loss specifically; magnesium is mentioned as an element whose effects vary by alloy and as a constituent affected by broader charge-design constraints. Consequently, the excerpt supports qualitative conclusions about accumulation, oxidation-related losses, and property risks, but quantitative answers would require separate experimental or industrial data for the specific alloy, tool material, melt temperature, atmosphere, fluxing practice, and number of remelts.

## 1. jarfors2026bifilmgenerationin pages 1-4 (Context ID: pqac-00000034)

Bifilm generation in metal handling and degassing:
Total numbers, sizes and damage

Anders E. W. Jarfors



 Jönköping University
Toni Bogdanoff
 Jönköping University


Research Article

Keywords: Oxide bifilms, aluminium casting, rotary degassing, melt transfers

Posted Date: September 8th, 2026

DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10838912/v1

License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
Read Full License

Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported.





                                                    Page 1/18Abstract

Oxide bifilms are increasingly recognised as the dominant defects governing the quality and
performance of cast aluminium alloys. However, conventional Reduced Pressure Testing (RPT) only
detects bifilms that inflate during solidification, thereby underestimating the true bifilm population. This
study develops a theoretical framework to quantify bifilm generation during two critical melt-treatment
operations: melt transfer and rotary degassing. Models based on Weber-number-controlled bubble
entrainment and breakup were used to estimate bifilm formation rates and characteristic defect sizes.
Under typical industrial processing conditions consisting of two melt transfers and rotary degassing, a
minimum bifilm concentration of 1,577 mm-3 was predicted, with melt transfer identified as the principal
source of defect generation. Experimental assessment of bifilm populations using focused ion beam
serial sectioning and three-dimensional reconstruction revealed approximately 187,500 hidden oxide
defects mm-3, exceeding predictions by more than two orders of magnitude. Incorporation of daughter-
bubble formation increased the estimated concentration to approximately 6000-8000mm-3, but a
substantial discrepancy remained, indicating that many bifilms likely pre-exist in primary aluminium
feedstock. A damage-factor model that combines defect size, numbers, and tensile specimen geometry
further demonstrated that melt-transfer operations are considerably more damaging than degassing.
Furthermore, degassing becomes more damaging at a certain rotation rate, supporting a change in
current rotary degassing practice.

1 Introduction
1.1 The bifilm issue

It is often stated that porosity is one of the main quality issues in cast aluminium components. However,
the origin and significance of porosity cannot be fully understood without considering oxide films,
commonly referred to as bifilms. Campbell [1] introduced the concept of bifilms and the bifilm index for
gravity die casting, and since then, there has been ongoing discussion about the importance of porosity
and bifilms.

Tiryakioglu [2] investigated the conditions for the nucleation of a hydrogen-induced porosity and
concluded that this was not feasible. Tiryakioglu [3], further analysed the connections between porosity
and hydrogen under reduced pressure. It was clearly shown that porosity levels could range from 0% to
20% at 6.7kPa and from 0% to 30% at 0.67kPa. All low values occurred in filtered material that was clean
and nearly “free” of bifilms. This explains the variations observed by Dispinar et al. [4], who showed that
the erratic correlation between hydrogen and the bifilm index is due to confounding by cleanliness and
hydrogen content. This is strong evidence that porosity and bifilms are intimately connected and that
porosity will not occur without bifilms.

Porosity and bifilm content are intimately connected. In the paper by Dispinar et al. [4], the bifilm index
and shrinkage were correlated with hydrogen content. In this paper, two alloys were investigated,


                                                    Page 2/18showing significant differences in shrinkage behaviour. It is seen that shrinkage was divided into
external and internal shrinkage. There was a weak tendency for the AlSi7Mg alloy to exhibit greater
internal than external shrinkage as hydrogen content increased, but no significant trend in total
shrinkage with hydrogen. In terms of the bifilm index, the spread in the index increased with the
hydrogen content, leaving no statistically significant difference between the hydrogen content and the
bifilm index, even though the tendency was that the bifilm index increased with the hydrogen content.
This suggests that hydrogen contributes to the formation of porosity, but that something else
determines the amount of internal porosity. The works by Uludaq et al [4] showed that there is no
relationship between the number density, pore size, and bifilm index for clean and melts with a low bifilm
index

The bifilm index has often been correlated to mechanical properties. Zhang et al. [5] showed that to
correlate the bifilm index, it is insufficient to measure the bifilm index in the conventional fashion. There
are two anomalies that need to be accounted for: 1) shrinkage pores and pore structure in proximity to
each other require being counted as one defect, and 2) larger crack-like features that do not open fully.
Their area and Feret diameter do not match the fully inflated pores [5]. This is due to their 3-dimensional
characteristic. A similar attempt at characterisation of the bifilms was made by Song et al [6]. They
found that the ratio between the bifilm defect volume and the corresponding assumed sphere defect
volume with the same surface area was mainly in the range of 0.2–0.8, meaning that the shape of the
defects was quite varied. An improved bifilm metric, the Bifilm spatial index, was also proposed.
However, no link to mechanical properties was established. This is because hydrogen may inflate or
grow pores, but bifilms/oxide films appear to control where pores form and why scatter occurs.
Bogdanoff et al. [7] used Focused Ion Beam (FIB) serial sectioning, which revealed that surface cracks
represented only a small fraction of the actual damage within the material volume. Multiple subsurface
cracks were detected that were not visible in conventional two-dimensional observations, and crack
coalescence occurred frequently below the polished surface. Three-dimensional reconstruction
demonstrated that the actual crack population was substantially larger than that estimated from surface
observations alone.

It is therefore understood that the bifilm index obtained from Reduced Pressure Testing (RPT) is widely
used as a measure of melt quality. However, the bifilm index only quantifies bifilms that have inflated
sufficiently during solidification to become visible as pores. Consequently, the measured bifilm index
represents only a partial fraction of the total number of bifilms. The total amount of bifilms in the melt
has not yet been properly determined

Olofsson et al. [[8]] showed that porosity and bifilms compete to limit material performance. Foremost, it
should be noted that pores act as stress concentrators, causing bifilms in their vicinity to open earlier
than in areas without pores. Olofsson et al [8] also concluded that the current quality assurance systems
based on porosity are outdated and insufficient to provide the required information on material quality
and performance.
1.2 Bifilm generation and handling

                                                    Page 3/18First, the nature of oxidation in aluminium melts must be determined. Wang et al [9], studied the
oxidation of aluminium melts experimentally. They found that an amorphous layer first formed, and from
this layer, γ-Al2O3 nucleates and grows as small particles. Prolonged oxidation results in further
transformation to α-Al2O3. Mayer and Tiryakioglu [10] did a molecular dynamics study of early oxidation,
confirming the findings of Wang et al [9]. When exposed, oxygen atoms penetrate into the upper layers of
the surface, along with some surface-adsorbed atoms. This leads to the transformation of the randomly
close-packed, layered surface into an amorphous alumina layer. This amorphous alumina layer is heavily
aluminium-rich (Al5O). This layer forms within a nanosecond and is unavoidable. Consequently, exposure
of molten aluminium to oxygen-containing environments results in the near-instantaneous formation of
an amorphous oxide layer.

The handling and removal of bifilms was critically reviewed by Cao and Campbell [11]. Sedimentation
processes are in practice limited to larger bifilms being nearly neutrally buoyant, and only with a
sufficient amount of entrained gas, they will float, impeded by form drag from the extended or
convoluted shapes [11]. Similarly, degassing is efficient at generating additional flotation, as the bifilms
expand as the gas content is reduced during passive degassing. Today, most degassing is performed by
rotary degassing, which aids the flotation of larger bifilms but generates a massive number of smaller
bifilms [11]. In addition, operating a rotary degassing equipment with vortex formation makes the
flotation ineffective, as it reintroduces the material that has floated into
